item.title: Judith Slaying Holofernes
item.lesson: The biblical heroine Judith, saving her people by beheading the Assyrian general Holofernes in his tent, was a common subject — but nobody painted it like this. Where other artists show Judith recoiling delicately from her own deed, Artemisia Gentileschi gives us the physics of the act: two women braced with their full weight, sleeves rolled, blood arcing onto the sheets, a job being finished. Gentileschi was the greatest of Caravaggio's followers and the first woman admitted to Florence's Accademia del Disegno; she built an international career in an era when women could rarely even train as painters. Her biography — including the rape trial in which she testified under torture against her attacker — has often threatened to swallow her art, but the paintings themselves make the argument: absolute technical command, put in service of women rendered as protagonists with agency, muscle, and will.
item.lookFor: Notice the sword: perfectly vertical, dead center of the composition — the painting is literally organized around the instrument of the act.
